'''''Melaleuca paludicola''''', commonly known as '''river bottlebrush''', is a plant in the myrtle [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Myrtaceae]], and is [[Endemism|endemic]] to eastern [[Australia]]. (Some Australian state [[Herbarium|herbaria]] continue to use the names ''Callistemon sieberi'' or ''Callistemon paludosus''.)<ref name=Udovicic>{{cite journal|last1=Udovicic|first1=Frank|last2=Spencer|first2=Roger|title=New combinations in ''Callistemon'' (Myrtaceae)|journal=Muelleria|date=2012|volume=30|issue=1|pages=23–25|doi=10.5962/p.292240 |s2cid=251007557 |url=http://www.rbg.vic.gov.au/documents/Muelleria_30-1_3_Udovicic_Spencer.pdf|accessdate=11 June 2015}}</ref> It is a shrub or small tree with flexible, often drooping branches, pinkish new growth and spikes of cream, pale yellow, or sometimes pink flowers in summer.

==Description==
''Melaleuca paludicola'' is a shrub or tree growing to {{convert|8|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} tall, with fibrous bark, or hard, fissured bark on older plants. Its leaves are arranged alternately and are {{convert|20-68|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long, {{convert|1.3-8|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide, flat, linear to narrow lance-shaped and have a small point at the end. There is a distinct mid-vein and 11–18 indistinct side veins.<ref name=Brophy>{{cite book|last1=Brophy|first1=Joseph J.|last2=Craven|first2=Lyndley A.|last3=Doran|first3=John C.|title=Melaleucas : their botany, essential oils and uses|date=2013|publisher=Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research|location=Canberra|isbn=9781922137517|page=267}}</ref><ref name=RBGS>{{cite web|last1=Spencer|first1=Roger|last2=Lumley|first2=Peter F.|title=''Callistemon sieberi''|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Callistemon~sieberi|publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney: Plantnet|accessdate=15 July 2015}}</ref><ref name=florabank>{{cite web|title=''Callistemon sieberi''|url=http://www.florabank.org.au/files/documents/provenance/20070810-01.pdf|publisher=Corangamite Seed Supply and Revegetation Network|accessdate=25 January 2018}}</ref>

The flowers are a shade of cream to yellow, occasionally pink and are arranged in spikes on the ends of branches which continue to grow after flowering and also on the sides of the branches. The spikes are {{convert|20-30|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} in diameter with 10 to 40 individual flowers. The petals are {{convert|2.6-4.2|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and fall off as the flower ages and there are 48–67 stamens in each flower. Flowering occurs mainly from October to January and is followed by fruit which are woody, cup-shaped [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]]s, {{convert|3-4.3|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long.<ref name="Brophy" /><ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="florabank" />[[File:Melaleuca paludicola habit.jpg|thumb|225px|Habit in the [[Gibraltar Range National Park]] ]]

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Melaleuca paludicola'' was named in 2006 by [[Lyndley Craven]] in ''[[Novon]]'' when he transferred ''Callistemon sieberi'' to the present [[genus]].<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca paludicola''|url=  https://biodiversity.org.au/boa/instance/apni/613698|publisher=APNI|accessdate=15 July 2015}}</ref><ref name=Novon>{{cite journal|last1=Craven|first1=Lyn A.|title=New Combinations in ''Melaleuca'' for Australian Species of ''Callistemon'' (Myrtaceae)|journal=Novon|date=2006|volume=16|issue=4|page=472|url=http://www.bioone.org/doi/abs/10.3417/1055-3177%282006%2916%5B468%3ANCIMFA%5D2.0.CO%3B2|accessdate=15 July 2015|doi=10.3417/1055-3177(2006)16[468:NCIMFA]2.0.CO;2|s2cid=84723155 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> ''Callistemon sieberi'' was first formally described by botanist [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle]] in 1828 in ''[[Prodromus Systematis Naturalis Regni Vegetabilis]]''.<ref name=APNI(2)>{{cite web|title=''Callistemon sieberi''|url=https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/523071|publisher=APNI|accessdate=25 January 2018}}</ref><ref name=Prodromus>{{cite book|last1=de Candolle|first1=Augustin Pyramus|title=Prodromus Systematis Naturalis, Volume 3Regni Vegetabilis|date=1828|location=Paris|page=223|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/7152#page/234/mode/1up|accessdate=21 July 2015}}</ref>
The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''paludicola'') is from the [[Latin]] word ''palus'' meaning "swamp", "marsh", "bog" or "fen"<ref name="RWB">{{cite book|last1=Brown|first1=Roland Wilbur|title=The Composition of Scientific Words|date=1956|publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press|location=Washington, D.C.}}</ref>{{rp|514}} and the suffix ''-cola'' meaning "inhabitant".<ref name="RWB" />{{rp|217}} An earlier, alternative name ([[Synonym (taxonomy)|taxonomic synonym]]) for the species was ''Callistemon paludosus'' and the present name was chosen to link with the earlier one.<ref name="Brophy" />

''Callistemon paludosus'' is regarded as a synonym of ''Melaleuca paludicola'' by the [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]].<ref name ="WCSP">{{cite web |url=http://wcsp.science.kew.org/namedetail.do?name_id=31468 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210227223558/http://wcsp.science.kew.org/namedetail.do?name_id=31468 |url-status=dead |archive-date=27 February 2021 |title=''Callistemon paludosus'' |work=[[World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]] (WCSP) |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Melaleuca paludicola'' occurs from [[Warwick, Queensland|Warwick]] in the far south east of [[Queensland]], through [[New South Wales]] as far inland as the eastern part of the [[North West Slopes|North West Plains]] to the eastern half of [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]].  There is a [[Disjunct distribution|disjunct]] population in the [[Mount Lofty Ranges]] and [[Adelaide]] districts of [[South Australia]].<ref name="Brophy" /><ref name="RBGS" /> It grows in and near rivers, in dry, rocky riverbeds and in flood channels subject to periodic inundation.<ref name="Brophy" /><ref name="florabank" />

==Use in horticulture==
''Melaleuca paludicola'' is sometimes cultivated as ''Callistemon sieberi''. An alpine form is a smaller, denser, rounded shrub suitable as a more formal plant.<ref name=Wrigley>{{cite book|last1=Wrigley|first1=John W.|last2=Fagg|first2=Murray|title=Australian native plants : a manual for their propagation, cultivation and use in landscaping|date=1983|publisher=Collins|location=Sydney|isbn=0002165759|page=193|edition=2nd}}</ref>
